Choose What to Sell

Choose What to Sell
===================

With the market mapped out, it’s time to move from possibilities to a decision. This is where ideas become tangible. Choosing what to sell isn’t about finding the one “perfect” product—it’s about picking a strong starting point you can build on.

Your first product will be your **anchor**. It doesn’t have to be huge, flashy, or complicated. What matters is that it’s clear, well thought out, and capable of carrying a story. From that anchor, your brand can expand naturally—coffee into mugs and teapots, soap into lotions and candles, clothing into accessories and homeware.

This module will walk you through how to list your ideas, narrow them down, check if the numbers make sense, weigh craft and quality, and create a quick prototype. By the end, you’ll have the confidence to commit—knowing your choice isn’t a gamble, but the result of careful thinking and real demand.

Launch and Learn

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Collect and Use Feedback

Collect and Use Feedback
========================

Every customer interaction is a chance to learn. Feedback—both positive and negative—is one of your most valuable resources. It tells you what’s working, what’s broken, and what opportunities you’re missing. The trick is to collect it systematically and then actually use it.

### **Where Feedback Comes From**

*   **Reviews** – Etsy, Amazon, or direct store reviews show what customers loved (or didn’t).
*   **Surveys** – Short Google Forms or Typeform surveys can dig deeper into customer experience.
*   **Emails & DMs** – Casual feedback in replies is often the most honest.
*   **Returns or Complaints** – Painful, but useful. They show you what needs fixing fast.

### **How to Use It**

*   **Spot Patterns** – Don’t overreact to one review. Look for repeated themes.
*   **Prioritize Fixes** – If multiple buyers mention shipping delays, fix logistics before launching new products.
*   **Highlight Wins** – Share positive feedback in your marketing—it builds trust and credibility.
*   **Fuel Innovation** – Suggestions from buyers can inspire your next product or bundle.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Create a simple system to collect feedback (spreadsheet, Notion board, or even a shared doc). After each batch of orders, add reviews and customer notes. Mark what’s a “fix,” what’s a “win,” and what’s a “future idea.”

See the Market Clearly

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Balance Passion With Proof

Balance Passion With Proof
==========================

Every great brand starts with something you care about. Coffee, skincare, handmade clothing — whatever excites you. Passion matters, because when things get hard (and they will), it’s what keeps you motivated. But passion alone isn’t enough. The other half of the equation is proof: proof that customers want what you’re offering.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/681891861c959d9ef7314a0a/68d5ab1f02025444fcadb449_Figure%201.3.webp)

_The sweet spot is where what you love overlaps with what people actually want. That’s where strong brands are born._

Plenty of people dream about turning hobbies into businesses. The ones who succeed are those who check the numbers first. For example, Etsy reports millions of monthly searches for “soy candles,” but only a fraction as many for “ceramic incense burners.” That doesn’t mean incense burners can’t work — but it does mean you need to know what you’re walking into.

The formula is simple: **choose a product that excites you, then back it up with evidence of demand.** If you love tea, check Google Trends or Amazon best-sellers to see which blends are rising. If you’re into clothing, look at Pinterest boards or TikTok hashtags for signals of what people are wearing. Proof keeps your passion grounded, and passion keeps your proof exciting. Together, they form a foundation you can actually build on.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Write down three product ideas you’re genuinely passionate about. For each one, spend 15 minutes checking search volume (Google Trends, Etsy search bar, or Amazon’s “best sellers”). Circle the one that shows both demand and excitement — that’s your sweet spot.

See the Market Clearly

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Collect Feedback Early

Collect Feedback Early
======================

It’s tempting to wait until everything is “perfect” before showing your product to anyone. But the truth is, the sooner you get feedback, the faster you can improve—and the fewer expensive mistakes you’ll make.

Feedback doesn’t have to be formal surveys or long questionnaires. Start simple:

*   Share your mockups with a few friends who actually buy similar products.
*   Post early packaging designs in a small online group (Reddit, Discord, or a Facebook group for your niche).
*   If you’ve set up a landing page, email the first signups and ask them what drew them in.

The point isn’t to collect compliments—it’s to uncover blind spots. People might say your font is hard to read, your price feels high, or your packaging doesn’t match the vibe of your product. That’s gold. You can use it to refine before going bigger.

And here’s the best part: early feedback creates early fans. The people you invite into the process often become your first customers. They feel like they’re part of the journey, not just bystanders.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one channel today (friends, online group, or email list). Share one concrete thing: a product idea, packaging draft, or landing page screenshot. Ask: “What do you like? What would you change?” Write down the top three answers you hear.

Choose What to Sell

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Commit With Confidence

Commit With Confidence
======================

You’ve explored the landscape, spotted trends, checked the margins, matched product to story, weighed craft and quality, and even built a prototype. That means you’re ready for the most important step: choosing your first product.

Think of this product as your **anchor**. It’s not the only thing you’ll ever sell—it’s the foundation you’ll build the rest of your brand around. A good anchor product gives you focus now, while leaving room for expansion later. Coffee can grow into mugs, grinders, and teapots. Soap can grow into lotions, scrubs, and candles. An apron can grow into an entire kitchenware line.

What matters is that you decide. All the research and planning you’ve done so far wasn’t busywork—it was a filter to make sure this moment is backed by real data, real demand, and your real passion. There’s no perfect product, but there is a product you can confidently start with, knowing it will carry your brand forward.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Circle one product idea today and call it your anchor. Write down one or two natural extensions you could add later. Then stop second-guessing—move forward with the knowledge that you’ve done the work to make a smart, sustainable choice.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Define Your Identity

Define Your Identity
====================

Every strong brand begins with a clear identity. This is the “why” that shapes everything else—from your logo and fonts to your packaging and tone of voice. Without it, design decisions feel random. With it, everything clicks into place.

Your identity has two layers:

*   **Brand Story:** What’s the narrative you want people to connect with? Maybe it’s about heritage craft, sustainability, or daily rituals.
*   **Brand Ethos:** What values guide you? Quality over shortcuts? Transparency? Playfulness? Serious craftsmanship?

Your voice flows naturally from these choices. A brand rooted in craft might speak with care and authority. A brand built on fun might use a light, witty tone. Either way, your story + ethos + voice form the backbone of the entire system you’re about to build. That system will extend across your messaging, your website, your packaging—everywhere your customer interacts with you.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Write a short identity statement in three parts: Our story is… Our ethos is… Our voice is… Keep it simple, one sentence each. This becomes the blueprint for every design choice ahead.

Build Your Digital Home

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Design a Landing Page

Design a Landing Page
=====================

Marketplaces like Etsy handle checkout, but you still need your own digital home—a branded landing page that introduces your product, captures emails, and funnels people to buy. Think of it as the polished front porch of your brand: simple, focused, and built to convert.

You don’t need to code this yourself. Tools like **Figma**, **Framer**, or **Webflow** make it easy to design and launch a clean page in a day. The key is structure. Every effective landing page follows a simple flow:

### **Core Sections of a High-Converting Landing Page**

1.  **Hero Section**  
    *   Big headline with your product’s promise.
    *   Strong image (product shot, lifestyle photo, or packaging).
    *   Clear CTA button (e.g. _“Shop on Etsy”_ or _“Join the Waitlist”_).
2.  **Features Section**
    *   3–4 key features of your product, each with a short description and icon or image.
3.  **Benefits / “Why Buy” Section**
    *   Explain what makes your product worth choosing—craft, quality, sustainability, story.
4.  **Testimonials Section**
    *   Quotes or reviews from early testers, friends, or your first customers. Social proof drives trust.
5.  **Strong Call to Action**
    *   Repeat the CTA button with urgency (_“Order Now”_, _“Get Yours Today”_).
    *   Add an **email signup form** so even if visitors don’t buy, you can reach them later.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Sketch your landing page structure in Figma (or use a Webflow/Framer template). Add your brand colors, fonts, and patterns. Keep it short and direct—one page, no distractions, just conversion.

Expand Your Product Line

Expand Your Product Line
========================

Once your anchor product is selling steadily, the next step is to grow your offering. Expanding your product line doesn’t mean chasing every idea—it means adding products that make sense alongside what you already sell. Done right, each new product strengthens your brand ecosystem and increases customer lifetime value.

### **Why Expand**

*   **Deeper Loyalty** – Customers who already love your anchor product are the easiest to sell to again.
*   **Higher Order Value** – Bundles and upsells boost revenue per customer.
*   **Brand Ecosystem** – Each product supports the story you’re telling, making your brand feel complete.

### **How to Expand Thoughtfully**

*   **Complementary Products** – Add items that naturally go with your anchor product.
    *   Coffee → mugs, grinders, gift bundles.
    *   Soap → soap dishes, lotions, travel sets.
    *   Candles → seasonal scents, holders, matches.
*   **Tiered Options** – Offer “entry level” and “premium” versions of your core product.
    *   Skincare → sample kits, full-size bottles, luxury packs.
*   **Seasonal or Limited Editions** – Introduce variety without changing your anchor.
    *   Tea → special winter blends, summer iced packs.

### **The Rule of Focus**

Expansion should feel like a branch growing from the same tree, not like planting a whole new forest. Keep everything tied back to your brand identity and ethos.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

List 3 natural extensions of your anchor product. Pick one to prototype next—something small and low-risk that your existing customers are most likely to buy.

Experiment With Ads

Experiment With Ads
===================

Organic content and influencer partnerships get you far, but sometimes you need a little extra push. Paid ads are the way to amplify your reach—but at this stage, think of them as **experiments**, not massive campaigns. Small tests can teach you what resonates before you scale.

### **Why Ads?**

*   **Instant reach** – You don’t have to wait for the algorithm to pick you up.
*   **Targeted audiences** – Ads let you reach people by interest, location, or behavior.
*   **Testing ground** – Ads show quickly which message, photo, or product attracts clicks.

### **Where to Start**

Stick with the channel you’ve already chosen. If you’re focused on Instagram, run Instagram ads. If you’re on TikTok, try TikTok Spark Ads. For X, test promoted posts. Consistency matters—you’ll learn faster if all your energy goes into one ecosystem.

### **How to Experiment Smartly**

*   **Start small** → Begin with $5–10/day. Enough to test, not enough to break the bank.
*   **Test creatives** → Run 2–3 variations of the same ad (different headline, image, or call to action).
*   **Track results** → Look at click-through rate (CTR), cost per click (CPC), and conversion.
*   **Kill losers, double winners** → Stop what doesn’t work, reinvest in what does.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Run one small ad campaign this week on your chosen platform. Set a daily budget cap. Test at least two creative variations. After 7 days, review performance and keep only what worked best.

Focus on One Channel

Focus on One Channel
====================

When it comes to marketing, it’s easy to spread yourself thin. You see competitors posting everywhere—Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube—and think you should do the same. But in the beginning, trying to master every channel means you master none. The smarter move is to **focus on one channel first**.

### **Why Focus Matters**

*   Consistency is easier on one platform.
*   You’ll learn faster from real engagement and feedback.
*   Your audience will know where to find you.

Once you’ve built traction, you can always expand. But first, you need to plant a flag.

### **How to Pick Your Channel**

Choose based on **your audience** and **your strengths**:

*   **Writers & storytellers** → start with **X (Twitter)**. Short posts, threads, and commentary thrive here.
*   **Visual thinkers** → start with **Instagram**. Great for product photography, patterns, packaging, and brand lifestyle shots.
*   **Talkers & performers** → start with **TikTok**. Perfect for live demos, behind-the-scenes clips, and personality-driven content.

The right channel is the one where your customers already hang out _and_ where you can show up consistently without burning out.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one channel today. Write down why it fits your audience and your style. Commit to posting there three times a week for the next month. Ignore the rest until you see traction.

Grow With Reviews

Grow With Reviews
=================

Nothing sells your product better than someone else saying it’s great. Reviews are the ultimate form of social proof—customers trust them more than any ad, and marketplaces like Etsy or Amazon rank you higher when you collect positive feedback. In the early days, reviews can make or break your momentum.

### **Why Reviews Matter**

*   **Trust** – Buyers believe other buyers more than they believe you.
*   **Visibility** – More reviews = higher placement in search results.
*   **Feedback Loop** – Reviews show you what’s working and what needs improvement.

### **How to Get Reviews**

*   **Ask politely** – A short message after a sale (or even a thank-you note in the package) makes a big difference.
*   **Make it easy** – Share the direct review link or remind them it only takes a minute.
*   **Reward loyalty** – Don’t pay for reviews (it’s against policy), but do send surprise thank-you notes, discounts, or early access to new products.
*   **Use negative reviews wisely** – Don’t panic. Respond professionally, fix the issue, and treat it as free advice to improve your product.

### **Use Reviews Everywhere**

Don’t just collect reviews—put them to work. Add them to your landing page, share them in newsletters, and highlight them on social posts. A single good review can become a marketing asset for months.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Write a short, friendly “review request” template. Use it in your post-purchase follow-ups and thank-you notes. Then, create a spot on your landing page or Etsy shop banner to showcase your best review once you get it.

Keep Consistent Branding

Keep Consistent Branding
========================

Once you’ve designed your visual system—colors, fonts, patterns, logo—the next challenge is consistency. A customer should feel your brand identity no matter where they meet you: on Etsy, your landing page, Instagram, or even in a product instruction sheet. Consistency builds trust. Inconsistency looks amateur and breaks the story you’ve worked so hard to create.

### **Where Consistency Matters**

*   **Landing Page** → carry over your fonts, colors, and logo from packaging.
*   **Etsy Shop** → make sure your banner, shop icon, and listing photos match the look of your landing page.
*   **Social Media** → keep a unified template for posts: same color accents, same font pairings, subtle background patterns.
*   **Marketing Materials** → PDFs, instruction guides, email headers—all should use the same palette and typography.
*   **Product Packaging & Inserts** → any thank-you notes, instruction cards, or promo flyers should feel like they belong with the product.

Consistency doesn’t mean repetition. It means every piece feels like it’s part of the same family. When your colors, fonts, and patterns show up everywhere, customers remember you faster and trust you more.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Create a simple “brand kit” file that includes your logo, font names, hex codes for your colors, and at least one repeatable pattern. Keep it handy, and apply it to every design—whether it’s an Etsy banner or a social post.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68375528de26944d4e4d088f_Home.svg)

Choose What to Sell

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

List Your Options

List Your Options
=================

Before you can choose what to sell, you need to see your options clearly. That means getting everything out of your head and onto paper (or screen). Think of it like a brainstorming session: no judgment, no filtering yet—just a wide-open list of possible products.

Your list can come from three main places:

*   **Passions**: What do you already love? Coffee, candles, clothing, skincare? Passion matters because you’ll be spending a lot of time with this product.
*   **Skills or Access**: What can you make, source, or design more easily than others? Maybe you already have a supplier contact, or a craft you’re good at.
*   **Market Gaps**: What have you noticed missing? A certain tea flavor you can’t find, a style of jewelry that isn’t represented, or a design that feels fresh.

Don’t overthink it yet. The point is to make the invisible visible. A list of 10–20 product ideas will give you raw material to refine in the next lessons. And don’t worry if some sound silly or impossible—often the best ideas start messy.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Set a 20-minute timer. Write down every product idea that comes to mind, big or small. Aim for at least 10. Keep them in a simple spreadsheet with three columns: Idea, Why I Like It, Where I Saw It.

See the Market Clearly

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Map the Demand

Map the Demand
==============

By now, you know the landscape, you’ve spotted some trends, and you’ve peeked at the competition. The next step is to make sure people actually _want_ what you’re planning to sell. This is where demand mapping comes in — figuring out where people are spending their money and how often they’re searching for products like yours.

Demand isn’t abstract. It shows up in search bars, reviews, and sales rankings. If people are searching “soy candle gift set” 50,000 times a month, that’s demand. If a niche Shopify shop has hundreds of reviews for handmade mugs, that’s demand. The trick is to map it across a few different channels so you’re not relying on one shaky data point.

Luckily, you don’t need to hire a market research firm. Free tools can give you a clear picture:

*   **Google Trends** shows search volume over time (are people more into matcha this year than last?).
*   **Etsy Search Bar** gives you autocomplete suggestions (a quick way to see what shoppers are typing most often).
*   **Amazon Best Sellers** shows what people are actually buying in real time.

Think of this as sketching a map. You don’t need to know every street. You just need the major roads that show where people are already traveling. Then you can decide if your brand wants to set up shop on that road — or on a smaller side street where traffic is lighter but less crowded.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one product idea and check it in three places: Google Trends, Etsy autocomplete, and Amazon Best Sellers. Write down the search terms and best-selling items that appear. Do you see steady demand? Seasonal spikes? A growing trend line? That’s your demand map.

Source With Care

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Negotiate Smartly

Negotiate Smartly
=================

Once you’ve found a supplier you like, the next step is to agree on terms. For new entrepreneurs, this is where nerves kick in. But remember: negotiation isn’t about “beating down” the supplier. It’s about finding a fair arrangement that works for both sides. A good supplier relationship should feel like a partnership, not a wrestling match.

Here are a few principles to guide you:

*   **Know your numbers.** If you’ve already checked margins, you know what you can afford. Walk into the conversation with those figures clear.
*   **Ask for clarity, not just price.** Confirm shipping costs, packaging details, lead times, and minimum order quantities (MOQs). Surprises later are much more expensive than asking upfront.
*   **Start small, negotiate later.** Don’t ask for big discounts on your first order. Prove yourself as a good client with consistent reorders, then you’ll have leverage to negotiate better terms.
*   **Be polite but firm.** Suppliers are more likely to give concessions to people they trust and enjoy working with. Push too hard early, and you may get cut corners on quality.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Draft a one-page “order outline” before you negotiate. List: unit cost target, MOQ, lead time, packaging requirements, payment terms. Use it as your checklist to keep the conversation clear and professional.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Pair Your Fonts

Pair Your Fonts
===============

Fonts are the voice of your brand in visual form. Just like tone of voice in writing, typography tells people if your brand is serious, playful, luxurious, or down-to-earth. A **font pairing** means choosing two (sometimes three) fonts that complement each other—usually one for headlines and one for body text.

Here’s the catch: you can’t just grab two random fonts and hope they look good together. Font pairing is an art. Some typefaces clash, others feel unbalanced, and some make your text hard to read. That’s why it’s best to use combinations that are already tested and proven.

### **How to Find Fonts**

Plenty of free tools make pairing simple:

*   **Google Fonts** – free library with built-in pairing suggestions.
*   **FontPair.co** – quick inspiration with ready-made pairings.
*   **Canva Font Combinations** – preview pairs directly in mock designs.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one expressive font for headlines and one simple, readable font for body text. Use one of the tools above to choose a pre-paired combination. Test it on a mock product label or landing page to see if it feels balanced and true to your brand story.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Pick Your Colors

Pick Your Colors
================

Color is one of the fastest ways to communicate your brand’s personality. A **brand color palette** is the set of colors you’ll use everywhere—your logo, packaging, website, and social media. It’s what makes your brand instantly recognizable.

Your palette should connect directly to your identity. A bold, energetic brand might use bright primaries. A craft-driven, heritage brand might lean on earth tones. A luxury brand might keep it minimal with black, white, and one accent. The key is consistency—once you choose your palette, stick to it across everything.

### **How to Build Your Palette**

You don’t need to guess. There are plenty of free tools that can generate palettes and help you test combinations:

*   **Coolors.co** – instantly generates palettes, lets you tweak and lock colors.
*   **Adobe Color** – explore harmonies and trending palettes.
*   **Canva Color Palette Generator** – upload an image (like a photo of your product or inspiration) and get a palette built from it.

A good palette usually has:

*   1 **Primary Color** (main identity)
*   2–3 **Supporting Colors** (backgrounds, accents)
*   1 **Neutral** (black, white, or gray tones to balance it out)

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Use one of the tools above to generate at least three palette options. Compare them against your identity statement from Lesson 1. Ask: Does this feel like my story? Would my customer connect with it? Pick one, and save the hex codes for future use.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Price With Purpose

Price With Purpose
==================

Pricing isn’t just math—it’s strategy. The number you choose tells customers how to perceive your product: is it everyday affordable, premium and aspirational, or somewhere in between? Set it too low and you undermine your craft. Set it too high and you risk scaring away early buyers. The goal is to price with purpose: a balance between profit, positioning, and customer trust.

### **Three Factors to Balance**

1.  **Costs** – Cover your product, packaging, shipping, and platform fees. If you don’t know your costs, you can’t price sustainably.
2.  **Market** – Look at what similar products sell for on Etsy, Amazon, or in shops. Pricing way below competitors hurts credibility; pricing far above requires a strong story to back it up.
3.  **Perceived Value** – Customers pay for more than the product—they pay for design, story, and quality. A beautifully packaged soap can sell for $12 where a plain one sells for $4.

### **Strategies That Work**

*   **Keystone Pricing** – A simple rule of thumb: retail price = 2x your total cost.
*   **Tiered Offers** – Offer small, medium, and premium versions (e.g. single item, bundle, gift set).
*   **Anchor Pricing** – Show a higher-priced option so your main product feels more accessible.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Calculate your total cost per unit (product + packaging + shipping + fees). Write down your competitors’ prices. Then decide: do you want to compete on accessibility, premium craft, or somewhere in between? Set your first price and commit to testing it.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Prototype Quickly

Prototype Quickly
=================

You don’t need a factory to test an idea. A prototype is simply the fastest, cheapest way to make your product real enough to learn from. The point isn’t perfection — it’s proof.

If you’re making coffee, that might mean a small batch of beans roasted by a local supplier and sealed in plain bags with printed stickers. For soap, it could be a handmade bar in sample molds. For clothing, it’s one piece sewn by a local tailor or a single manufacturer sample.

The sooner you hold a prototype in your hands, the sooner you can see what works and what doesn’t: texture, packaging fit, print clarity, even how customers react. Don’t wait for “final” — early prototypes save time, money, and frustration later.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one product and create a prototype within the next two weeks. Keep it small: 10 sample bags, 5 soap bars, 1 garment. Photograph it, share it with a few people, and note their reactions.

Source With Care

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Prioritize Craftsmanship

Prioritize Craftsmanship
========================

When it comes to sourcing, the cheapest option is rarely the best one. What sets great brands apart isn’t shaving pennies off the cost—it’s choosing suppliers who value **craftsmanship**. A product that feels well made earns trust, and trust is what keeps customers coming back.

Take Moroccan teapots. The ones made by skilled Moroccan craftsmen—using real metalwork, traditional designs, and durable materials—last for years and carry a beauty that tells a story. Compare that to the machine-made knockoffs churned out in bulk in China: thin metal that dents or breaks, toxic materials that leach into your tea, and designs that look “almost right” but lack the soul of the original. One feels authentic, the other disposable.

The same applies to consumables. True **oud wood** is carefully sourced and naturally aromatic, its scent deep and complex. Cheap substitutes, on the other hand, are just scraps of wood sprayed with synthetic oud oil—flat, one-dimensional, and gone in minutes.

Craftsmanship is about more than aesthetics—it’s about safety, sustainability, and fairness. Suppliers who value craft tend to respect their materials, their workers, and the environment. Choosing them may cost a little more, but it makes your brand part of a bigger story: one of care and authenticity instead of shortcuts.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Ask your shortlisted suppliers: How are your products actually made? Who makes them? What materials are used? Do they cut corners with cheaper substitutes? Write down the answers, and cut any supplier who can’t prove they value craft and fairness.

Secure Reliability

Secure Reliability
==================

A good sample doesn’t always mean a reliable supplier. Many look great on the first order, then stumble once production scales up. That’s why the final sourcing step is to secure reliability: making sure your supplier can deliver the same quality, on time, again and again.

Reliability is about more than the product. It’s about communication, consistency, and accountability. Some suppliers send their best work for samples, but then cut corners later. Others accept your order but pass it off to a lower-tier subcontractor. That’s why you need to look beyond the item in your hand and test the partnership itself.

Here’s how to secure reliability:

*   **Ask about capacity.** Can they handle your order size now, and larger orders later?
*   **Confirm timelines in writing.** Get clear commitments on production lead time and shipping windows.
*   **Check responsiveness.** How quickly do they reply to your questions? A slow supplier now will be slower when things go wrong.
*   **Request consistency checks.** Ask how they ensure quality from batch to batch.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Place a small “trial order” after testing samples—big enough to test their process, but small enough to limit your risk. Pay close attention to timing, quality consistency, and communication. This trial run will tell you if they’re a long-term partner or just a one-time supplier.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Plan and Launch Campaigns

Plan and Launch Campaigns
=========================

A great product and a polished store won’t sell themselves. You need a campaign—a focused burst of attention that puts your offer in front of people and motivates them to act. Think of a campaign as a story with a start, middle, and end, designed to turn awareness into sales.

### **Keep Campaigns Simple**

At this stage, your first campaigns don’t need to be huge or expensive. A basic campaign might include:

1.  **Theme** – Tie it to a story, season, or event (e.g. _“Your New Morning Ritual”_, _“Holiday Gift Sets”_).
2.  **Channel** – Use the one platform you’ve focused on (IG, TikTok, X, etc.) for consistency.
3.  **Timeline** – Plan a clear beginning, middle, and end—launch week, follow-ups, final push.
4.  **Assets** – Photos, posts, emails, maybe one ad—all aligned with your theme and story.

### **Campaign Flow Example**

*   **Day 1**: Announce your product/offer with a strong hook.
*   **Day 3**: Post a behind-the-scenes story.
*   **Day 5**: Share a customer testimonial or early review.
*   **Day 7**: Send a final “don’t miss this” email or post.

### **Why It Works**

A campaign gives you focus. Instead of random posts or emails, you’re guiding customers through a short journey that builds excitement, answers questions, and ends in a clear call to action.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one theme for your first campaign (holiday, daily ritual, gift bundle, etc.). Write a 7-day outline with at least three posts and one email. Use your existing photos and copy—no need to overcomplicate.

See the Market Clearly

See the Market Clearly
======================

Every strong business begins with clarity. You can’t build a brand in the dark—you need to understand the terrain before you choose your path. That means looking at the big picture, spotting the waves of change, balancing what excites you with what people actually want, and learning from the competitors who are already out there.

This module is about sharpening your vision. You’ll map demand across platforms, run small experiments to test the waters, and learn how to gather feedback before you’ve spent serious money. Each lesson is designed to push you a step closer to certainty: certainty that your idea has potential, that your market exists, and that you’re not just building on hope.

By the end, you’ll have more than just an idea—you’ll have proof. You’ll know the landscape you’re stepping into, the trends worth paying attention to, and the signals that tell you customers are ready for what you’re offering. In other words, you won’t just _see_ the market—you’ll see your place in it.

Share Your Story

Share Your Story
================

At this stage, you’ve built a product, packaged it beautifully, and launched your digital home. Now it’s time to tell the world. Storytelling isn’t fluff—it’s how people connect with your brand, trust your product, and decide to buy.

In this module, you learned how to:

*   **Focus on one channel** so your energy builds traction instead of spreading thin.
*   **Work with influencers** who already speak to your audience and can authentically showcase your product.
*   **Experiment with ads** as small, low-risk tests to amplify your reach.
*   **Nurture with newsletters** so new subscribers walk through your story step by step until they’re ready to buy.
*   **Grow with reviews** to build trust and visibility that snowballs over time.
*   **Sell direct** so you gradually own more of the customer relationship and rely less on marketplaces.

The common thread? Every touchpoint carries your story forward. Whether it’s a post, an email, or a review, you’re guiding people through a journey of discovery—until buying from you feels natural, even inevitable.

Sell Direct

Sell Direct
===========

Marketplaces are the perfect place to start—but they’re not the final destination. Over time, the goal is to own your customer relationship fully. That means selling direct: through your own website, email list, or even private community.

### **Why Move Toward Selling Direct**

*   **More Control** – You own the checkout flow, the customer data, and the margins.
*   **Lower Fees** – Marketplaces take a cut; direct sales give you more per order.
*   **Brand Ownership** – Customers remember your brand, not just “an Etsy shop.”
*   **Loyalty** – Direct channels let you build long-term relationships without algorithm changes in the middle.

### **How to Start**

*   **Simple Site** – Tools like Shopify, BigCommerce, or even Webflow/Framer let you launch a branded shop quickly.
*   **Email-Driven Sales** – Use your newsletter list to drive customers straight to your own checkout page.
*   **Exclusive Offers** – Create bundles, limited editions, or early access products available only on your site.
*   **Gradual Transition** – Keep selling on Etsy/Amazon to capture organic traffic, but nudge loyal customers toward your own store over time.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Add one “direct offer” to your newsletter or landing page—whether it’s a bundle, an exclusive product, or free shipping. See how many customers choose to buy from you directly.

Shoot Great Photos

Shoot Great Photos
==================

Great product photos don’t just show your product—they sell it. On Etsy or any marketplace, photos are the first thing people see. Crisp, well-lit images can make the difference between a scroll-past and a sale.

### **Option 1: Do It Yourself**

Your smartphone is more than enough if you follow a few basics:

*   **Lighting:** Use natural light near a window, or set up soft diffused light. Avoid harsh shadows.
*   **Background:** Keep it clean and simple—white, neutral, or lightly styled. Don’t clutter the frame.
*   **Angles:** Shoot at least 3–5 angles (front, side, detail, in use).
*   **Editing:** Use built-in apps (Apple Photos, Google Photos) to adjust brightness, contrast, and crop. Keep colors true to life.

### **Option 2: Light Retouching**

If your shots are good but need a polish, hire quick retouching on **Fiverr** or **Upwork** for under $50. Small tweaks (removing dust, balancing color) can make a big difference.

### **Option 3: Professional Photography**

If you want polished lifestyle shots or perfectly staged images, consider product photo services like **Pixelz**, **Soona**, or local photographers. Costs vary, but you’ll get magazine-quality results that set your brand apart.

### **Option 4: Use Supplier Photos**

Sometimes suppliers provide decent photos. If they’re clean, high-resolution, and match your brand’s vibe, you can start with them. Just be cautious—many supplier photos are generic or AI-generated (as we saw in sourcing), so make sure they actually reflect your product.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick your path: DIY photoshoot, quick Fiverr retouch, or professional service. Aim to have at least 5–7 photos per product listing: a hero shot, multiple angles, one in-use or lifestyle shot, and a close-up detail.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Source the Packaging

Source the Packaging
====================

Designing your packaging is only half the job. The other half is sourcing materials and finishes that bring your design to life—and make sure it feels as good as it looks. Cheap packaging can undo all the work you’ve put into your brand system. Thoughtful sourcing makes your product stand out and builds trust with customers.

### **Elements to Consider**

*   **Central Frame (Sticker or Label):** Your logo and product info often live on a sticker or label that sits inside the frame. Choose durable, smudge-proof stock that holds up in handling.
*   **Patterned Wrapping Paper:** If your packaging uses a full pattern, this could be printed wrapping paper, tissue, or box wrap. Make sure it’s repeatable and printed cleanly.
*   **Paper Quality:** Not all paper is equal. Compare matte vs. glossy finishes, thickness (GSM), and recycled or sustainable options. A flimsy box makes a brand feel cheap; sturdy paperboard or kraft instantly feels premium.
*   **Debossing & Embossing:** These techniques press your design into the paper (deboss = sunken, emboss = raised). Subtle, tactile details that elevate your brand.
*   **Foil & Metallic Print:** Gold, silver, or colored foils can make logos, frames, or accents shine. Best used sparingly for luxury or premium feel.
*   **Printing Techniques:** Offset vs. digital printing can affect color depth, sharpness, and cost. Ask suppliers for samples before committing.
*   **Sustainability:** Customers notice when you choose recycled paper, soy-based inks, or biodegradable wraps. These choices add authenticity to your brand story.

The key is to treat packaging as part of the product, not an afterthought. Every texture, finish, and detail should reinforce the story you’re telling.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Request physical samples of paper stocks, stickers, and finishes from at least two packaging suppliers. Compare how each feels in your hands. Write down which ones align with your brand ethos (craft, quality, sustainability).

Source With Care

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Start Small

Start Small
===========

When you’ve found a supplier you trust, it’s tempting to go big right away. But the smartest move is to **start small**. Small orders let you test everything—production, shipping, quality, and customer response—without putting too much money at risk.

Suppliers may push for larger minimum orders, but you usually have more room to negotiate than it seems. Many will allow smaller runs for a higher unit price. That’s okay. Paying a bit more upfront is better than being stuck with boxes of inventory you can’t sell or that reveal hidden flaws too late.

Starting small also gives you flexibility. You can test different variations, refine your packaging, and get early customer feedback before scaling up. Each small batch becomes a learning round—proof that your system works.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Place your first order at the smallest viable size. Track every part of the process: how long production takes, how the shipment arrives, how the product feels in customers’ hands. Use this data to decide whether to scale, tweak, or pivot.

See the Market Clearly

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Test the Waters

Test the Waters
===============

So far, you’ve circled an idea that excites you, checked the competition, and mapped out demand. But knowing the market is one thing. Seeing if _your version_ of the idea clicks with real people is another. That’s where testing the waters comes in.

Testing doesn’t mean investing thousands in inventory. It means running small, low-risk experiments to see if people respond. You can:

*   Put up a **landing page** with photos or mockups (made in Figma or Canva) and a simple email signup form.
*   Run a **tiny ad campaign** (as little as $20–50) on Instagram or TikTok to see if anyone clicks.
*   Offer a **limited pre-order** on Etsy with a long ship date, just to gauge interest.

The goal isn’t to make money yet. The goal is to answer: “Do people notice? Do they care enough to click, sign up, or even buy early?” If you get traction, you know you’re onto something. If not, you can adjust quickly without wasting resources.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one of the three methods above and test your idea this week. Measure how many signups, clicks, or pre-orders you get. Even a handful is a green light to keep moving. Zero response? That’s valuable too — it tells you to refine your product or story before going further.

Share Your Story

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Work With Influencers

Work With Influencers
=====================

Influencers are today’s word-of-mouth marketers. A single shoutout from the right person can put your product in front of thousands of potential customers who already trust that voice. But here’s the key: **focus only on influencers in the channel you’ve chosen.** Don’t scatter your energy trying to reach Instagram influencers if you’re building on TikTok, or TikTok creators if your traction is on X. Stay aligned.

### **How to Approach Influencers**

*   **Start small.** Micro-influencers (1k–10k followers) often have stronger engagement than mega-influencers.
*   **Look for authenticity.** Their audience should genuinely match your niche, not just big numbers.
*   **Engage before asking.** Like, comment, and share their posts before sliding into DMs. Show real interest.
*   **DM with value.** Keep it personal and professional. Offer to send your product, explain your story, and suggest how it could benefit their audience.

### **Build Long-Term Relationships**

Don’t think of influencer marketing as a one-off shoutout. The best results come from repeated, authentic mentions over time. Treat influencers as partners. Send them new product launches, ask for honest feedback, and reward their support with early access or exclusives.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Identify 5 influencers in your chosen channel whose audience overlaps with yours. Start engaging with their content this week. Draft a DM that introduces yourself, shares your story briefly, and offers them your product with no strings attached.

Track With Analytics

Track With Analytics
====================

You can’t improve what you don’t measure. Analytics tell you where your customers come from, what they do on your site, and how often they buy again. At this stage, you don’t need a giant data team—you just need the basics set up so you can track what matters most.

### **Where to Add Analytics**

*   **Landing Page** → Add a free tool like Google Analytics or Plausible to see who visits, where they come from, and what actions they take.
*   **Etsy / Amazon** → Both platforms offer built-in analytics dashboards to track visits, conversions, and search traffic.
*   **All-in-One Dashboards** → Tools like Google Looker Studio or Triple Whale can combine data from multiple sources into one simple view.

### **The Five Metrics That Matter Now**

1.  **Traffic Sources** – Where visitors come from (social, search, email, direct).
2.  **Conversion Rate** – % of visitors who buy or sign up.
3.  **Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)** – How much it costs you to get a customer (ads, promos).
4.  **Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)** – How much an average customer spends over time.
5.  **Churn Rate** – How many customers never come back after the first purchase.

Focusing on these five helps you see what’s working and what needs fixing without drowning in data.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Install Google Analytics (or an alternative) on your landing page, and connect your Etsy/Amazon analytics. Create a simple dashboard—start with traffic sources, conversions, CAC, LTV, and churn. Update it weekly to spot trends.

Build Your Funnel

Build Your Funnel
=================

Your brand story doesn’t just live in one place—it flows. A funnel is how you guide people step by step, from discovering you to becoming loyal customers. Without it, you’re leaving too much to chance.

### **A Simple Funnel That Works**

1.  **Social Media Touchpoint** – A post, story, or video sparks interest.
2.  **Landing Page** – Visitors click through to learn more about you.
3.  **Email Capture** – Even if they’re not ready to buy, you get their email.
4.  **Newsletter Journey** – A series of emails introduces your story, values, and products.
5.  **Conversion** – When the timing feels right, you link them to your Etsy storefront (or Amazon).

This funnel works because it’s gentle. Instead of shouting “buy now,” you guide people: connect first, share your ethos, then ask for the sale once they know you better.

### **Keep It Simple**

You don’t need dozens of steps. A clear landing page, a signup form, and a basic 3–5 email sequence can be enough to move someone from curious to customer.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Sketch your funnel on paper. Write down what your first social media post might say, what the landing page headline should be, what lead magnet you’ll offer, and what your first 3 emails would contain. Then set up a basic funnel using your email tool of choice (Mailchimp, ConvertKit, or Beehiiv).

Choose What to Sell

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Check the Margins

Check the Margins
=================

It’s one thing to love a product idea. It’s another to make sure it can actually make you money. That’s where margins come in. A margin is the difference between what it costs you to make (or source) a product and what you can realistically sell it for.

Margins don’t have to be complicated math. Here’s the quick way:

*   **Find your cost**: Add up the product cost + packaging + shipping to you.
*   **Estimate your price**: Look at competitors selling similar items on Etsy or Shopify. What are they charging?
*   **Do the subtraction**: Price – Cost = Margin.

As a rough rule:

*   Under 30% margin → too tight for a small brand.
*   40–60% margin → comfortable for most consumer products.
*   Over 60% margin → strong, gives you flexibility for ads or wholesale later.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Take your 3–5 shortlisted products and run the quick margin check. Write down cost, price, and margin for each one. If an idea looks great creatively but the margin is weak, flag it. Strong margins give you the breathing room to grow.

Source With Care

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Compare Local and Global

Compare Local and Global
========================

Once you’ve identified reliable suppliers, the next question is: should you source locally or globally? Both options come with trade-offs, and the right choice depends on your product, your budget, and your brand values.

**Local suppliers** give you speed, accountability, and often higher consistency. Shipping is cheaper and faster, communication is easier, and you can often visit the factory or workshop. If your brand emphasizes craft, sustainability, or “made local” authenticity, this can become part of your story. The downside? Local suppliers usually cost more, and your product selection may be limited.

**Global suppliers**—often based in Asia, Eastern Europe, or Latin America—can offer lower costs and greater variety. They’re well-suited for products that need scale from the beginning. But you face longer lead times, tariffs, and higher shipping costs. Timing becomes crucial: delays at ports or customs can derail a launch. And since your end customer may be in another part of the world, you may need to bridge the gap with third-party fulfillment centers to keep delivery times reasonable.

Neither path is “better” across the board. The trick is to know your priorities. Do you need the fastest turnaround and tightest control? Local might be the way. Do you need to stretch your budget or access more specialized categories? Global may open doors.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

For your anchor product, compare one local and one global supplier. Write down the differences in cost, lead time, shipping, tariffs, and minimum order size. Ask: which option matches your brand story, and which one fits your growth stage?

Launch and Learn

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Craft an Offer That Lasts

Craft an Offer That Lasts
=========================

A single product with a price tag isn’t enough. What you really sell is an **offer**—a combination of product, positioning, and value that feels irresistible to customers. The best offers aren’t one-off gimmicks; they’re built to last, forming the backbone of your business as you grow.

### **What Makes an Offer Strong**

*   **Clarity** – Customers know exactly what they’re getting and why it matters.
*   **Value Beyond Price** – It’s not just the product, it’s the story, the design, the packaging, the experience.
*   **Longevity** – The offer makes sense today and will still make sense when you expand your line later.

### **Offer Structures That Work**

*   **Bundles** – Combine products for higher perceived value (e.g. coffee + mug, soap + dish).
*   **Subscriptions** – Consumables like coffee, tea, or skincare work beautifully in monthly plans.
*   **Limited Editions** – Seasonal or themed versions that add excitement without reinventing your brand.

### **Build Around Your Anchor Product**

Your first product should be the **anchor**—the core that you can build an ecosystem around. For example:

*   A coffee bag → leads to mugs, grinders, gift bundles.
*   A handmade soap → leads to soap dishes, lotion, gift sets.
*   A candle → leads to seasonal scents, holders, or subscription boxes.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Write down your anchor product, then list 2–3 natural extensions. Sketch a simple bundle or subscription that could turn your product into a long-term offer, not just a one-time purchase.

Connect Email Signups

Connect Email Signups
=====================

If you could only pick one marketing channel to own, make it email. Social platforms rise and fall, ads get more expensive, but an email list is yours forever. It lets you reach both people who haven’t bought yet and customers who already love your product. That makes email the core of any sales funnel.

### **Why Email Matters**

*   **For potential customers** → Capture emails from people who are curious but not ready to buy yet. They may not click “purchase” today, but if you stay in touch, they’ll be more likely to buy tomorrow.
*   **For repeat customers** → Email keeps them in your orbit. Announce new products, share special offers, or remind them when it’s time to restock. Loyal customers often generate more revenue than first-timers.

### **Capturing Emails on Your Landing Page**

Your landing page isn’t just a bridge to Etsy. It’s also a chance to collect emails. Don’t just ask for them—_earn_ them. Offer something valuable in exchange:

*   **Coffee Brand Example** → Downloadable guide: _“5 Coffee Blend Recipes You Can Make at Home.”_
*   **Skincare Brand Example** → _“Your Morning Ritual: A 7-Step Health & Skincare Routine.”_
*   **Homeware Brand Example** → _“How to Set a Table That Impresses Guests.”_

These freebies, often called lead magnets, invite people to join your brand’s story—even if they’re not ready to buy yet.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Add an email signup form to your landing page. Create one simple piece of downloadable content related to your niche. Test it with your first visitors, and start building your customer funnel from day one.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Create Your Logo

Create Your Logo
================

Your logo is the face of your brand. It’s the first impression, the shorthand that tells people who you are before they read a single word. The key is to design a logo that reflects your identity—the story, ethos, and voice you just defined.

### **Types of Logos to Consider**

Your brand’s character will point you toward the right style:

*   **Wordmark:** Clean text spelling your brand name. Great for modern, minimal brands.
*   **Initials / Monogram:** Letters inside a crest or mark. Works well for heritage or premium vibes.
*   **Geometric Symbol:** Simple shapes or patterns. A strong fit for bold, design-forward brands.
*   **Abstract Icon:** Flexible shapes that feel unique but not literal.
*   **Calligraphic Mark:** Scripted or stylized lettering, best for craft-driven or cultural brands.
*   **Logo + Mark Combo:** Text plus a small icon, versatile across packaging and digital use.

### **How to Get It Made**

You don’t have to design from scratch—there are paths for every budget:

*   **Template platforms** (like Canva or Envato) → quick and cheap, best for very tight budgets.
*   **Freelancer platforms** (Fiverr, Upwork) → you can contract a designer directly, often for $50–300.
*   **Curated design sites** (Dribbble, Behance) → higher-end designers who deliver more polished work, usually $500+.

Pick the route that matches your budget and ambition. Remember, your logo doesn’t have to be expensive—but it does need to feel aligned with your brand identity and flexible enough to use everywhere (website, packaging, social media).

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Pick one logo style that fits your story and ethos. Then decide how you’ll get it made: template, freelancer, or designer. Write down your choice and your budget ceiling before moving forward.

Launch and Learn

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Delegate Fulfillment

Delegate Fulfillment
====================

At the start, you’ll probably be packing boxes yourself—printing labels, sealing packages, and dropping them at the post office. That’s normal, and it teaches you the nuts and bolts of how your product moves. But as orders grow, fulfillment can eat up all your time. To scale, you’ll need to delegate.

### **Why Delegate?**

*   **Save Time** – Focus on design, marketing, and growth instead of taping boxes.
*   **Increase Consistency** – Professional fulfillment services handle storage, packing, and shipping at scale.
*   **Expand Reach** – Many fulfillment partners can ship faster, internationally, and with better rates than you can on your own.

### **Options for Fulfillment**

*   **Third-Party Logistics (3PL)** – Companies like ShipBob, ShipMonk, or Flowspace handle storage, packing, and shipping.
*   **Marketplace Fulfillment** – Amazon FBA or Etsy’s partnerships integrate directly with your storefront.
*   **Hybrid** – Keep some fulfillment in-house for special orders or local sales, and outsource the rest.

### **When to Switch**

*   You’re spending more time packing than selling.
*   Customers expect faster shipping than you can provide.
*   You’re running out of storage space at home.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Research one fulfillment partner that integrates with your marketplace (Etsy/Amazon) or future direct store (Shopify/BigCommerce). Request quotes for your product size and volume. Compare them to your current costs and time.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Find Your Patterns

Find Your Patterns
==================

Patterns are the invisible glue of great design. A subtle, repeatable background pattern can lift packaging, websites, and social media visuals from plain to polished. The most elegant brands use patterns not as decoration, but as a system—something that can be applied consistently across touchpoints to create a recognizable look.

### **Types of Patterns**

Patterns come in many styles, each carrying its own mood and cultural resonance:

*   **Arabesque / Islamic Geometry** – repeating geometric or floral motifs, timeless and highly versatile.
*   **Rococo** – ornate swirls and flourishes, perfect for luxury or heritage vibes.
*   **Japanese** – clean, repeating motifs like seigaiha (waves) or asanoha (hemp leaf), ideal for minimalist craft.
*   **Chinese** – intricate knotwork or cloud motifs, often bold and auspicious.
*   **Playful / Niche Repeats** – quirky icons or illustrations (e.g. coffee beans, soap bubbles, tiny aprons) that bring fun to casual brands.

Whatever style you choose, the key is **systematic design**. Patterns should repeat seamlessly, scale well, and feel like part of your identity. Done right, they become a quiet signature—something your customers recognize without even seeing your logo.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Browse free pattern libraries (like HeroPatterns, Patterninja, or Vecteezy) or commission a custom one. Save at least two seamless patterns that fit your brand identity, one geometric and one organic, and test them as a background on a mock package or web section.

Source With Care

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Find Your Suppliers

Find Your Suppliers
===================

Choosing what to sell is only half the battle. Now you need to figure out where your product will actually come from. This is where many first-time entrepreneurs stumble—because the internet is full of supplier directories that look shiny on the surface but hide a mess underneath.

Platforms like **Alibaba, Global Sources, and DHgate** list thousands of manufacturers, but most aren’t vetted. Many are middlemen, some inflate their capabilities, and yes—scammers are common. You’ll see tricks like:

*   **AI-generated product photos** that don’t match what they actually produce.
*   **Layers of middlemen**, each taking a cut, so you never know who’s really making your product.
*   **Premium products reserved for “favorite clients,”** while new customers get downgraded versions.
*   **Orders quietly handed off** to lower-tier subcontractors, so quality tanks without warning.

Posting in supplier forums or replying to random messages is even worse. When you don’t know who you’re dealing with, you risk poor quality, missed deadlines, and wasted money.

The rule is simple: **never rely on anonymous forms or faceless listings.** The safest route is to work with suppliers who have been vetted and come with warm points of contact. That means:

*   Finding **vetted supplier directories** that review and rate their members.
*   Joining **trade associations** or **industry groups** where suppliers are screened.
*   Asking for **referrals from other entrepreneurs** who’ve already ordered successfully.
*   Making sure you can reach a **real person**—someone with a track record, reviews, and accountability.

A supplier isn’t just someone who makes your product. They’re a partner in your brand’s reputation. If they cut corners, you pay the price. Choose carefully, and you’ll have a foundation that scales smoothly instead of collapsing under poor quality.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Start by browsing the Diraya Supplier Directory. Then, supplement it with 1–2 vetted directories in your category. Never proceed unless you can connect with a real, accountable contact on the other side.

Nail Your Brand Design

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Design the Packaging

Design the Packaging
====================

This is where everything you’ve created—your logo, colors, fonts, and patterns—comes together on the product itself. Packaging isn’t just a container. It’s your brand’s stage, the first thing customers see and touch. Done right, it tells your story in an instant.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/681891861c959d9ef7314a0a/6a54eee8f70e5d1447753e8e_figure-4.6.webp)

_Bring it all together: pattern in the background, logo in the central frame, colors and fonts applied consistently._

### **The Anatomy of Great Packaging**

1.  **Background Pattern** – the subtle repeatable design you chose in the last lesson. This sets the mood and gives your packaging texture.
2.  **Central Frame (or Medallion)** – the centerpiece that organizes everything. It can be geometric (circle, rectangle, hexagon) or ornamental (arabesque, crest).
3.  **Logo Placement** – your logo sits inside the central frame, acting as the anchor.
4.  **Typography** – your font pairing goes to work here:  
    *   Headline / Product Name (expressive font).
    *   Supporting Text / Description (readable font).
5.  **Colors** – apply your palette consistently: background hues for the pattern, accent tones for the frame, and neutral or contrasting colors for text.

Think of it as a hierarchy: background pattern sets the stage, the central frame holds the focus, and your logo + text deliver the message.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Create one packaging mockup for your anchor product. Use your pattern as the background, your palette for colors, your chosen fonts for text, and place your logo in a central frame. Don’t worry about final print specs yet—just make sure it feels cohesive and true to your brand identity.

Launch Your Storefront

Launch Your Storefront
======================

If all the design, packaging, sourcing, and identity work you’ve done so far were the makeup and wardrobe, launching your storefront is stepping up on stage. It’s how people find you, interact with your brand, and start buying. The smart move at first is to use a marketplace—for example, **Etsy** (especially for creative, craft, and lifestyle goods)—and once you’ve got traction, you can build your own custom e-commerce site on Shopify, BigCommerce, or similar platforms.

### **Why Start With a Marketplace First**

*   **Lower upfront cost**: Etsy has minimal setup fees (e.g. listing fees, transaction fees), whereas building and maintaining a standalone site (hosting, themes, plugins) can cost more early on. Etsy is cheaper for getting started.
*   **Built-in audience**: Etsy already has users who come looking for handmade, craft, unique, or gift items. Less effort is needed to attract traffic than launching a brand-new store from scratch.
*   **Ease of operations**: Payment processing, checkout, marketplace rules—all handled for you. You can start with fewer technical and operational hurdles.

Then, once you have a few sales, good reviews, and steady traffic, a custom storefront gives you more control: over branding, UX, margins, and perhaps when you want to scale or branch into wholesale

### **Tools & Tutorials**

*   **How to open an Etsy Shop:** Etsy’s Seller Handbook gives step-by-step: visit _Etsy.com/sell_, set your shop’s language, country, and currency, choose a name, etc. ([Etsy Help](https://help.etsy.com/hc/en-us/articles/115015672808-How-to-Open-an-Etsy-Shop?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
    ⁠)
*   **How to Start an Etsy Shop:** Walks through the steps, costs, tips for naming, branding, etc. ([IONOS](https://www.ionos.com/digitalguide/online-marketing/online-sales/how-to-start-an-etsy-shop/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
    )
*   **Etsy vs Amazon Comparison:** Helps decide which marketplace is best for your product category and growth goals. ([Printful](https://www.printful.com/blog/etsy-vs-amazon?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
    )

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/68d43aa2f88e9f6d6d4a580b_check-circle.svg)

Action

Decide right now which platform you’ll launch on first (probably Etsy). Use one of the tutorials above to set up your storefront this week. Make 2 live listings with your product photos, descriptions, and tags. Then, collect feedback from the first few customers / viewers and prepare to adjust after your first 5-10 sales.

Know the Laws

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Know Fitt's Law

**Know Fitts’s Law**
====================

_Fitts’s Law_ is a fundamental principle in human-computer interaction and ergonomics, formulated by psychologist **Paul Fitts** in 1954. It predicts the time it takes for a person to move to a target area (such as a button or link) based on two key factors:

*   The **distance** to the target
*   The **size** of the target

In simple terms, **the closer and larger a target is, the easier and faster it is to click**.

‍

Why It Matters in Design
------------------------

Fitts’s Law is critical when designing interfaces that are fast, efficient, and user-friendly. It encourages designers to:

*   Place important buttons and links in easy-to-reach areas (like corners or screen edges)
*   Make interactive elements large enough to be easily tapped or clicked
*   Minimize unnecessary movement between frequently used controls

‍

### Example in Practice

Think of a smartphone: the bottom navigation bar has large, easily tappable icons because thumbs can reach them quickly — a perfect application of Fitts’s Law.

By understanding and applying Fitts’s Law, designers can create interfaces that feel natural, responsive, and intuitive.

‍

Know the Laws

Know Hick's Law

Know Hick's Law
===============

_Hick’s Law_ (also known as the Hick–Hyman Law) is a principle from psychology and human-computer interaction that states:

> **“The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.”**

Named after British psychologist **William Edmund Hick**, the law shows that when users are presented with too many options, they take longer to decide — and may feel overwhelmed or frustrated.

‍

### Why It Matters in Design

Hick’s Law teaches us to streamline decision-making by:

*   **Reducing clutter**: Present only the most essential options to the user.
*   **Grouping related choices**: Use categories or progressive disclosure to simplify decision paths.
*   **Prioritizing clarity**: Make choices visually distinct and easy to scan.

‍

### Real-World Example

Think about a simple website homepage with just a few clear navigation links versus a cluttered page full of buttons. The clean design allows users to act faster and more confidently.

By applying Hick’s Law, designers and communicators can reduce cognitive load, improve usability, and guide users to take quicker and better-informed actions.

Know Jacob's Law

**Know Jacob's Law**
====================

_Jacob's Law_ of internet user experience, introduced by usability expert **Jakob Nielsen**, states:

> “Users spend most of their time on other websites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.”

‍

This law highlights the importance of familiarity in design. Instead of creating entirely new user interface patterns, designers are encouraged to:

*   Follow established web and app conventions.
*   Keep navigation and layout consistent.
*   Minimize user learning curves by aligning with common user expectations.

‍

By applying Jacob’s Law, you enhance usability, reduce friction, and increase user satisfaction.

Know the Laws

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66572ea1e52b0a26510b004d/681f82f97cf65c69f5998498_Chevron%20right.svg)

Know Miller's Law

Know Miller's Law
=================

_Miller’s Law_ is a cognitive psychology principle introduced by psychologist **George A. Miller** in 1956. It states:

> “The average person can only hold about **7 (plus or minus 2)** items in their working memory at one time.”

This means that people generally struggle to process more than **5 to 9 pieces of information** simultaneously.

‍

### Why It Matters in Design and Communication

Understanding Miller’s Law helps designers, educators, and communicators create content that aligns with human cognitive limits. Key takeaways include:

*   **Chunk information**: Break down complex content into smaller, manageable groups.
*   **Simplify choices**: Limit the number of options presented at once (e.g., in menus or forms).
*   **Use grouping and hierarchy**: Organize content in a way that visually supports memory and comprehension.

‍

### Real-World Example

Phone numbers are typically grouped (e.g., 123-456-7890) to make them easier to remember — a direct application of Miller’s Law.

By applying Miller’s Law, you make your content easier to understand, remember, and act upon.
